paragraphs: I

He was penniless and proud. Harnessed together, that pair does not pull a man towards pleasant places. There is only one thing that can stop them once they take the bit between their teeth: a woman. So there, you might say, is the theme of the story of Jonathan Drake, of Dunnabridge Farm, a landholding in the Forest of Dartymoor. To the Duchy, it was Naboth’s vineyard, and that greedy body would undoubtedly have paid a very fair price for it. But the Drakes held their land, refused to part with it, and boasted of owning fifty acres outright in the very middle of the Forest. They prospered, too, kept up with the times, and held their heads high for more generations than I can recall. Then they came to what all families, noble or ordinary, come to sooner or later: a black sheep to lead the flock. Every generation of a family will have its bad ones, but the trouble begins when one of them happens to be at the top. If the head of the family is a drunkard, a spendthrift, or too free and easy for this workaday shop of a world, the next generation had better look out for squalls, as sailors say.

Jonathan’s grandfather did the damage at Dunnabridge. Sport was in his blood through his mother’s side, and horses brought him to trouble. He bet on them and was ruined. His son then bred them and did not do much better. When both men dropped out of the hunt and died with their backs to the wall, one after the other, it seemed the game was over for those who came next. Fortunately, though, Tom Drake had only one child, a boy: the Jonathan I am telling you about. When his father and grandfather died within a year of each other, Dunnabridge was left to Tom’s widow and her son, then twenty-two. She wanted to sell it and leave Dartymoor. The place had treated her badly, and she hated the sight of it. But Jonathan, proud even then, asked the lawyers to look into matters. They told him Dunnabridge did not have to be sold, though selling might ease his finances and smooth his future. The Duchy particularly wanted the place and had offered what it was worth. Jonathan’s mother sided with the Duchy and went down on her knees to beg him to sell, but he refused. Sometimes he got a bee in his bonnet. He said all the Drakes would rise from their graves in Widecombe churchyard and haunt his every rising and lying down if he sold merely for his own convenience, to be rid of the place. So he arranged terms with the creditors. It turned out that his father and grandfather had owed nearly a thousand pounds between them, and Jonathan actually set out to repay every last penny. It took years of work, but by thirty-three he had done it. Only his mother could have told what it cost in scrimping and scraping. She never did, though, for she died two years before the final payment. Some even said her son’s miserly habits had hurried her to the grave. For all I know, they may have done. Certainly she had a better time while her husband lived. Tom was generous, full of life and easygoing. He liked meat on the table and plenty to wash it down. He loved Mercy Jane Drake dearly. When he died, leaving her was the only thought that troubled him. His last advice to his son was to sell Dunnabridge and take his mother off the Moor, down to the lower country she had come from.

But Jonathan was made of different stuff. Old people who had known several generations of the family said he took after an ancestor called Brimpson Drake. This long-dead man had been a miser and the richest of the family. He lived when we were at war with France and America, when Princetown sprang up and a great war prison was built there to cage all the fellows captured through our many victories at sea. Miser Brimpson was said to have made thousands by helping wealthy prisoners escape. His story, as it was handed down, mixed truth with falsehood. But one part seemed fairly certain: when the miser died and Dunnabridge went to his horse-racing cousin, no living person ever saw a penny of his fortune. Some said it was all nonsense, and he had never had any money, only pretended to. Others insisted he knew only too well who would follow him at Dunnabridge and hid his money so that no Drake would get it. He hated his heirs as only a miser can.

That was how matters stood when Mercy Jane died and Jonathan was left alone. He paid all his relatives’ debts, and for his pains he had his trouble and the honour of being honourable. Everyone respected him enormously. Still, a few of his mother’s friends always said it was a pity he had put his dead father’s good name before his living mother’s life. But we are not all built on the same pattern, and only fools waste their time blaming someone for being himself.

Jonathan went on his stern way. Then, in the lonely days after his mother’s death, when he lived at Dunnabridge with only two farmhands and a pair of sheepdogs, something suddenly entered his narrow view. There might still be other women in the world, even though his mother had left it. No doubt he also discovered that a home without a woman is merely a cruel mockery of what a home should be.

Quite a few people watched to see what Jonathan would do about this, and no doubt a young woman here and there took an interest too. He might be terribly poor, but he was not bad-looking, although his jaw was rather hard and his manner rather abrupt and stern towards people and animals alike.

Then began his strange courtship—if you can call it courtship when a poor man indulges in pride at the wrong moment and makes a spectacle of himself as a result. That is my view, at least. But you should know that quite a few people, as wise as I am, took the other side. They thought Jonathan covered his name in glory when he changed his mind about Hyssop Burges. That was her bitter name, but no pleasanter girl ever walked on shoe leather. She was Farmer Stonewer’s niece at White Works. He had taken her in out of charity and always said it was the best day’s work he had ever done. She was honest, hardworking and cheerful, with nothing especially remarkable about her except a fine figure and a proud way of holding her head high and looking people in the eye. Proud she certainly was, and very particular about her friends. But something in Jonathan struck like flint against her steel. He knew she was penniless, or he would never have looked at her twice. After a short, fierce sort of courtship, she accepted him. Everyone was pleased except Farmer Stonewer, who could not bear the thought of losing Hyssop, although his wife had been warning him for four years that it was bound to happen.
One evening the farmer and the girl sat waiting for Jonathan. She was a little nervous, and he was trying to calm her.
“Jonathan must be told,” she said. “This can’t go on any longer.”
“Then tell him,” said her uncle. “Good heavens! To look at you, anyone would think this was the worst news that could ever come between two poor lovers, instead of the best.”

“I know him much better than you do,” she told the farmer, “and I know how maddeningly difficult he can be about money. He nearly broke off our engagement when, in a weak moment, I asked him to let me buy my own engagement ring. He went as red as a turkey’s wattles and said I’d insulted him. Now, when he hears the secret, I can’t for the life of me guess how he’ll take it.”

“It’s a pity you didn’t tell him when he proposed,” Hyssop’s aunt declared. “He’s as proud as a silly peacock and terribly afraid of seeming to seek money, or even to look where it lies. But he came to you without knowing anything about the windfall. He loved you for yourself, like an honest man, and you loved him the same way. You know perfectly well that if your old cousin had left you five thousand pounds instead of five hundred, Jonathan Drake would still have been the right man for you. He can’t blame himself. Not a soul on Dartymoor except us three has ever heard of the money.”

“But he’ll blame me for having money at all,” she answered. “A dozen times before he proposed, he said he’d never look at a woman who had more cash than he did. That’s why I couldn’t bring myself to admit it and lose him. After we were engaged, it became harder still.”
“Why not wait until you’re married, then?” asked Mrs Stonewer. “You’ve waited so long already. Wait a little longer and surprise him with the news on your wedding night. Eh, James?”

“No,” the farmer answered. “‘Enough is as good as a feast.’ That would waste your blessings at such a time. Save the news for some rainy day, when he’s wondering how to get around a tight corner. That’s the moment to tell him, and the moment when he’s least likely to pull a face at the news.”

But Hyssop would not put it off any longer. She said she would have no more peace until the secret was out. That very night, when Jonathan came over from Dunnabridge for a little courting, they had the farm parlour to themselves. Finding him in a very kindly mood, she blurted it out. They rarely cuddled, for he was not built that way. But now and then he would agree to sit beside her with his arm around her, when she picked up his hand and drew it into place. From time to time she rubbed her cheek against his mutton-chop whiskers until ordinary politeness obliged him to kiss her.

Well, Hyssop got it out—God alone knows how, as she said afterwards. She got it out and told him that an old, aged cousin had died and left her a nice little sum of money. She had never touched a penny, but had let it grow in the bank. She hoped and prayed it would help them at Dunnabridge. Of course, he must manage it, since he was a man and so very clever with such things. She went on and on, quite afraid to stop and hear his reply. But after repeating it all about a dozen times, she ran out of breath. She closed her mouth, tried to smile, and looked up at Jonathan anxiously and pleadingly.
His hard grey eyes bored into her like a pair of small drills. In answer to all her talk, he asked just one question.
“How long have you had this money?” he said.
She told the truth, faltering and trembling under his glare.
“Four years or more, Jonathan.”
“That’s years and years before I asked you to marry me?”
“Yes, Jonathan.”
“And you remember what I said about never marrying anyone who had more than I have?”
“Yes, Jonathan.”
“And you know perfectly well how often I told you that, after paying all my father’s debts, I had nothing left, and it would take years to build up anything you could call money?”
“Yes, Jonathan.”

“Very well, then!” he cried, lowering his brow and clenching his fists. “Very well! You’ve deliberately deceived me. If you would do that about one thing, you would do it about another. I’m leaving this house this instant, and you can tell your relatives why. I’m terribly sorry, Hyssop Burges. No man will ever love you better than I did. You would have lived to find that out once all this courting foolishness was over and you were my wife. But now I’ll have nothing to do with you, because you’ve played games with me. So—so I’ll say goodbye!”

He walked straight out without another word, and she staggered, weeping, to her uncle and aunt. They could not believe their senses. Jimmy Stonewer declared that any man who could make such a masterpiece of a fool of himself as Jonathan had that night was better off unmarried. He told Hyssop she had made a wonderful escape from a prize idiot, and his wife agreed. But she could not see it that way. She knew Jonathan was not a prize idiot. His raging pride did not anger her; she admired it enormously. Seeing what an unusually proud and haughty man he was only made her feel her loss more cruelly. Plenty of other men would have married her, and twice as many again if they had known about the money. But beside her hawk of a Jonathan, they all seemed as tame as robins. She had plenty of devil in her too, when it came to a fight. Now, while he merely said they had broken off the match over a difference of opinion and gave no reason, she set to work with all her strength to win him back. She used her wits, sharpened by love, as well as she knew how, to outwit him into marriage.
II

In truth, she made little progress. Jonathan was always polite afterwards, but trying to win him back through gentleness and affection was like trying to melt an iceberg with a box of matches. Kindness could not win him. He felt he had treated the world better than it had treated him, and the thought shrivelled his heart a little. You might call him always shy and suspicious. Yet beneath that, he was as honourable, upright and high-minded a man as you could wish to meet. Hyssop loved him as she loved her own life, and after their sad quarrel her health suffered a little. Then, by chance, she was taking the train from Princetown to Plymouth to see a chemist and get something to give her an appetite. Who should be in the very same carriage but Mr Drake and his farmhand, Thomas Parsons?
Other people were there too. An old fellow who had known Jonathan’s grandfather brought up the story of Miser Brimpson and asked young Drake whether he believed any of it.

Naturally, Jonathan dismissed such foolishness. He told the old fellow not to talk nonsense like that in the ear of the nineteenth century. But when Jonathan and Parsons got off at Yelverton station, Hyssop, who knew the old man, asked him for more about the miser. He explained, as well as he could, that Brimpson Drake had made untold thousands from the French and American prisoners. Without a doubt, he said, it was all still hidden at Dunnabridge.

“Of course Jonathan’s too clever to believe such a story, just like his father. But his grandfather believed it. The old fellow spent half his time poking around the farm. Unfortunately, he had no luck. But it’s there, for certain. If Jonathan had enough faith, he would find it. Not by digging and wasting time and effort, but by doing what is right and proper in such matters.”
“And what would that be?” asked Miss Burges.
Just then, however, the Plymouth train arrived, and the old man said he would explain another time.

“This generation laughs at such things,” he said. “But those who laugh last laugh best. For all we know to the contrary, nothing but his conceit and pride stands between that stubborn young man and the wealth of a bank.”

Hyssop thought a great deal about this. But she did not need to visit the old man again as she had intended. When she got home, her uncle, Farmer Stonewer, knew all about the matter. He told her that the previous generation firmly believed a miser’s spirit could never leave its hidden hoard until the money was brought to light and returned to human hands.

“Millions in good money have been found that way, if everything we hear is true,” declared Farmer Jimmy. “And if one miser has been known to walk, which nobody can deny, why not another? Those who believe in such dark things—and I don’t say I do, and I don’t say I don’t—those who know such mysteries have happened within their own memory or their friends’, would doubtless say Miser Brimpson still creeps around his gold now and then. If that money is anywhere within Dunnabridge Farm, and if Jonathan were looking out on the right night at the right moment, the odds are he might see his ancestor sitting over his moneybags like a hen over a clutch of eggs. Then he could recover the hoard.”

“But such a thing needs faith,” Mrs Stonewer told her niece, “and that pig-headed creature has none. He’s too proud to believe in anything he doesn’t understand. Lucifer was just the same before him. If you told Jonathan this, he’d rather let the money go than deliberately set out to hunt a ghost. Yet there it is. A humbler sort of man, with the Lord on his side and trust in his heart, might very well recover all those tubs of money the miser acquired.”
“Then he would have thousands against my poor tens,” Hyssop said. “Not that he would ever come back to me now, I suppose.”

Still, from the look in Jonathan’s eyes when they met, she knew he loved her yet. His foolish, proud heart still hungered for her, though he would rather have been dragged under a harrow than show a spark of what burned there.
So, using this nonsense about buried treasure, she set her brains to work again. She wanted to see whether Miser Brimpson’s ghost might offer a way out of her trouble.

Until the story reached me, only those who helped her knew what she did. But it was the cleverest thing I ever heard of a young woman doing, and it worked a wonder. In fact, I can see only one objection to the scheme, though it was serious for her. There had to be a secret between Hyssop and her husband, and she kept it as close as the grave until the grave itself closed over him. Yet it was an innocent secret. After all, there is hardly one married couple in five hundred in which each has not locked away one little cupboard and thrown away the key.

Six months passed. Jonathan worked as only he knew how, trying to forget his bitter disappointment through toil. He worked early and late, got permission to reclaim a piece of moor as a new enclosure, and added a very decent three acres to his farm. Around this time he noticed that Parsons, his farmhand, kept bringing up Miser Brimpson Drake. At first Jonathan laughed. Then he grew angry and ordered Thomas to be quiet. But obedient and humble as Parsons was, he kept returning to the subject. He told how his father had known a man whose own brother was a miser. Three nights after the miser’s burial, that brother had seen him, as plain as truth, in the chimney corner of his room. They searched and found, less than three feet from where the ghost had stood, a place in the wall containing seventeen gold sovereigns and a white witch’s cure for glanders. Thomas Parsons swore to this on the Bible. He said it was a certain fact that New Year’s Night was when most misers walked, and advised Jonathan not to shut his eyes to his own interests.

“At least, as a thinking man who believes in religion and the powers of the air, as the Bible calls them, you might give it a chance,” Thomas said. Jonathan told him to shut his mouth and stop disgracing Dunnabridge with such childish nonsense.
The next autumn Jonathan went beyond Exeter to buy some black-faced, horned Scottish sheep. He wanted Parsons to accompany him, but the man fell ill the night before, so young Hacker went instead.

Drake decided that Thomas Parsons would have to leave. Dunnabridge was no place for sick people, and he meant to dismiss the old fellow when he returned. But Thomas was better by the time his master came home, so the dismissal was dropped. Jonathan merely told Tom that if he fell ill again, it would be the last time. Parsons said that was only right. But he hoped that, at his age—only sixty-five or thereabouts—his breathing would not trouble him again for at least ten years. He added that he had done his work as usual while the master was away. He did not mention that Hyssop Burges had dared to call at Dunnabridge with a pony and cart. She had spent quite a long time there, looking all over the house and farmyard, among other places, before driving away.
Jonathan himself told the next part of the story to his two men on the first day of the following year.

There was little morning light yet. The three of them sat in the Dunnabridge kitchen by candlelight, putting away bread and bacon and a quart of tea. Thomas noticed his master was eating almost nothing. Instead, Jonathan went to the barrel and drew a pint of ale. He took it to the peat fire and put his boots as close to the embers as he dared without burning them.
“What’s wrong?” asked Thomas. “Don’t tell me you’re ill, master. If you are, I reckon nothing weaker than brandy will bring you round.”
“I’m not ill,” Jonathan answered shortly.
He seemed unsure whether to go on. Then he decided to.
“There was a man in the yard last night,” he said. “If I thought either of you knew anything about it, I’d dismiss you this instant, before you’d got the bacon down your throats.”
“A man? Surely not!” cried Parsons.
“Why didn’t the dog bark?” asked Hacker.

“How the devil do I know why he didn’t bark?” Jonathan answered, dark as night, staring into the fire. One side of his face was red from the flames. The other was steel-blue in the daylight just beginning to filter through the window.

“All I can tell you is this,” he added. “I went to bed at half past ten, just after that pair of old fools at Brownberry went off to see in the New Year. I slept until midnight. Then something woke me with a start. I can’t say what, but no doubt some loud noise close by. I was dropping off again when I heard more noise, a steady sound repeated over and over. At first I thought it was owls, but then I heard that it wasn’t. You might have thought someone was thumping a barrel. At any rate, I woke, sat up, and realised the sound came from the yard.

“Then I looked out of my bedroom window. The moon was as bright as day, and the stars sparkled too. Down by ‘the Judge’s Table,’ where the thorn tree grows, I saw a man standing beside the old barrel as plainly as I see you two now.”

“The Judge’s Table” is a wonderful curiosity at Dunnabridge. If you go there, you should ask to see it. It is a great slab of moorstone, said to have come from Crokern Torr, where the tin miners held their parliament in ancient times. Now it rests over a water trough, with a hawthorn tree rising above it.
Having reached that point, Jonathan paused for breath, took his pipe from his pocket and lit it. Then he drank half the beer, spat into the fire and continued.

“A man as tall as me, if not taller. He wore one of those old white beaver hats, and a flowing white beard as long as my plough horse’s tail. He walked up and down, up and down over the stones, like a sailor walking up and down a ship’s deck. I shouted to him, but he took no more notice than the moon. Up and down he went. Then I told him that if he wasn’t gone in two minutes, I’d get my hunting gun and fire. Still he paid no attention. I don’t mind telling you men that, for half a second, I felt a creeping chill and gooseflesh down my back. But I reckon it was only the cold. My window was wide open, and I had been leaning out for quite a while into ten degrees of frost.

“After that I grew angry. I went downstairs, lifted the gun from its hooks above the mantelpiece, and ran out just as I was, in nothing but my boots and nightshirt. At first the hour was as still as the grave. The moon shone on the river far below and lit the eaves and windows. Then, through the silence, I heard Widecombe’s bells ringing in the New Year. But the old night-bird in his top hat had gone. He hadn’t left a hair of his beard behind. I looked around, and then the dog came up, barking furiously. He didn’t recognise me in those clothes until he heard my voice. That’s the story, and I’d very much like to know who that curious old rascal is.”
At first neither man answered, and the daylight grew stronger. Then old Parsons spoke, wagging his head and swearing that his master had seen no man, but a creature from the other world.

“I’ll stake my life,” he said, “that you saw Miser Brimpson’s ghost walking. I’ll swear by the New Year that it was his way of showing where his belongings are buried. For God’s sake, if you don’t want trouble with unknown creatures, go and pull up the cobblestones and see whether there’s anything underneath.”

Jonathan acted as though it was all nonsense and would not let either Thomas or Hacker move a pebble. But the following day he visited a very old man named Samuel Windeatt. Windeatt’s father had been a boy in the days of the War Prison and was said to have seen and known Miser Brimpson alive. The old man declared that he had heard of the miser in his own childhood, and that Brimpson certainly wore a beaver hat and had a white beard a yard long. Jonathan came home more thoughtful than before. Finally, though he said he was ashamed to do it, he let Tom persuade him. Two days later the three men set to work where Drake had seen the ghost.

They dug and dug, this way and that. Jonathan found nothing. Parsons found nothing. But Hacker came upon a box. They dragged it from the earth and found another just like it underneath. The pair looked like old, rotten wooden chests, made from boards fastened with rusty nails. They had no locks or keys, but that did not matter: they fell apart at a touch. Inside was a quantity of plated ware—candlesticks, candle snuffers, tea kettles, table silver and the like.
“Thunder!” Jonathan cried. “It’s all pewter rubbish, not worth a five-pound note! We’ll dig again.”
And dig they did, for a week, until that part of the farmyard had been turned over like a trenched kitchen garden. But they did not find another teaspoon.
Meanwhile, someone who understood such things explained to young Drake that the objects were neither pewter nor Britannia metal. They were old Sheffield plate, and worth plenty of good money.

Jonathan was too bewildered by the event to do anything for a month. Then he went to Plymouth with a few pieces in his bag. The man he showed them to was so interested that he insisted on coming to Dunnabridge to see the whole collection. He offered two hundred and fifty pounds in cash, there and then, which made it quite clear to Jonathan that the things must be worth a good deal more. They haggled for a week. Finally Jonathan went to Exeter and got another dealer to name a price. In the end, the two dealers divided the collection between them, and Jonathan came away with a clear three hundred and fifty-four pounds.
III

He did not much like talking about his good fortune, and inquisitive people got little out of him. Parsons and Hacker, of course, talked freely and often: it was the greatest adventure of their lives. By telling the tale over and over, old Parsons eventually came to speak as though he had seen the ghost himself.

Then, after thinking it over for three or four months, when spring had come again, Jonathan Drake went to White Works one night, just as he used to when courting Hyssop Burges. The little party was there as usual: Mrs Stonewer knitting, the farmer reading yesterday’s newspaper, and Hyssop sewing in her place beside her aunt.

“Well!” said Farmer Jimmy. “Wonders never cease! Seeing you here again is almost as great a wonder as the story of the old miser’s tea things. I’m sure we all congratulate you, Jonathan. I needn’t tell you how very pleased we were to hear about it.”
The young man thanked them very politely. He said it was a curious turn of events, and even now he hardly knew what to think about it.

“I would put it down to some nonsense I’d dreamed,” he said. “But money is money, and who knows that better than me? On that same subject, I’d like a few words with Hyssop, if she’s willing to give me ten minutes of her time.”
“You’re welcome, Mr Drake,” she said.

He started at the surname. But she got up, and they went to the parlour just as usual. There she sat in her old corner of the horsehair sofa and looked at him. He did not sit down, at least not at first. He paced fiercely and spoke fiercely.

“I’ll ask one question before I go on. If the answer is what I fear, I won’t trouble you again,” he said. “In a word, are you engaged again? I suppose you are. You’re not the sort who lacks offers. If it’s so, say it quickly, and I’ll go and trouble you no more.”
“No, Mr Drake. I’m as free as the day you—you rejected me,” she answered in a very quiet little voice.

He snorted, but was far too thankful to quarrel with her words. She could see he was becoming very excited. He paced back and forth with shorter and shorter strides, like a hungry caged tiger that knows its piece of horsemeat is on the way.
At last he burst out again.
“A lot of lies have been told about that old plate we found at Dunnabridge. The truth is that I sold it for three hundred and fifty-four pounds.”
“That’s what Tom Parsons told Uncle. It’s a wonderful thing. We sat up all night talking about it, Mr Drake.”
“For God’s sake, call me Jonathan!” he cried. “And tell me—tell me how much you inherited. You must tell me. You can’t keep it back. It’s life or death—to me.”
She had never seen him so excited, but knew very well what was in his mind.
“If you must know, you must,” she answered. “I thought I told you when—when—”
“No, you didn’t. I wouldn’t stay to hear. Whatever it was, you had more than me, and that was all I cared about. But now, if by good fortune it’s less than mine, you understand—”
“Of course it’s less. A hundred and eighty pounds and the interest—a little over two hundred altogether—is what I have.”
“Thank God!” he said.
Then he asked whether she could still marry him, or whether she knew too much about his ways and ideas to want to.
And she accepted him again.

You see, Hyssop Burges was my mother. When Father died, she told me the true story. By then the old people at White Works and Tom Parsons had all gone to their last home, and the secret was safe enough with Hyssop herself.

The great difficulty was to put more than half her money straight into Jonathan’s hands without his knowing where it came from. Even after they thought of the ghost trick, it was hard to find a clever way to do it. Hyssop wanted to hide gold sovereigns at Dunnabridge. But her uncle very shrewdly pointed out that they would all bear dates. They could never have managed to find three hundred or more sovereigns a hundred years old. Then old Thomas, who was in the secret, of course, suggested trinkets and jewels. He played Miser Brimpson and received five pounds for doing it so cleverly, then another five from his master after the objects were found. Finally Mrs Stonewer, who had a friend in the business, said Sheffield plate would do the trick. She was right. They bought the plate for three hundred and eighty pounds and kept it hidden at White Works until they learned Jonathan intended to leave for several days. Then my mother drove it across. Thomas made the cases from old, rotten boards. They dug a slanting hole beneath the cobblestones and put everything neatly back in place long before young Drake came home.

“Jonathan and I married that autumn,” my mother told me when she related the tale. “The next New Year’s Night, he was at our bedroom window as the clock struck twelve. He stayed there for an hour, looking into the yard as keenly as the hawk he was. He thought I must be asleep. But I knew perfectly well he was looking for an old man in a beaver hat with a long white beard. And I knew perfectly well he would never see him again. Of course, your father took good care not to tell me the next morning that he’d been watching for the ghost.”

In her own last days, my mother often dwelt on that trick. Sometimes, as the time drew nearer and nearer for her to meet Father again, she said, “I wonder whether it will make any difference in heaven, where no secrets are hidden?” Knowing Father as well as I did, I felt very sure it might make an enormous difference. So, in my crafty way, I avoided a direct answer. I told Mother that, for my part, I was certain some secrets would not be allowed to come out even on Judgement Day, for fear of turning heaven into the other place. This, I said, was one of them. But that always troubled her.

“I want it to come out,” she would say. “If Jonathan doesn’t know, I shall certainly tell him. I’ve kept it in long enough, and I can’t trust myself to keep doing so. He has to know. With all eternity to get over it and forgive me, I have a right to hope he will.”
Hyssop Drake died determined to do that. I certainly hope that when my turn comes to join my parents again, I find no shadow between them. But there is plenty of room for doubt—knowing Father.
